metadata.title: Using machine learning techniques for evaluating creativity in Graphic Combination Task (GCT) among Chinese college students

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses an online, researcher-developed Graphic Combination Task (GCT) administered to a recruited sample of Chinese college students, not an international large-scale assessment microdata file. The manuscript does not report any complex survey design, sampling weights, or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it does not provide any weight variable names. Because the analysis is based on a convenience/recruited sample and ML models trained on task process features, the appropriate “weight” concept here is not a survey representativeness weight. For replication or extension, researchers should treat the sample as non-survey data unless a probability sampling design and corresponding weights are explicitly documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study predicts creativity scores derived from expert ratings and process-derived features from an online task; it does not use PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes from an ILSA framework. Missing-data handling is not described as an explicit imputation/deletion strategy for model training inputs/labels; instead, the paper reports data cleaning and exclusion of invalid responses (72 invalid participants). Given that the dependent variables are continuous creativity scores and the paper does not document how any remaining item/feature missingness was handled, the missing-data strategy is a reporting gap for ML reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were recruited online to complete the GCT plus two criterion-validation tasks. Data cleaning was conducted by two graduate students to eliminate responses deemed meaningless, random, or left blank; 72 participants were excluded as invalid, yielding 700 valid participants (overall validity rate 90.67%). For criterion validity, 300 of the 700 valid participants were randomly selected for the Improvement Toy Task and Picture Completion Task. For Study 2 model training/evaluation, the 700 participants’ process data were split into a training set (70%) and a testing set (30%).

main_findings.dataset_used: GCT online task (Study 2; Chinese college students)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted Ensemble — R²: 0.71, RMSE: 0.10 (vs MLR R²: 0.71 RMSE: 0.11; CatBoost R²: 0.70 RMSE: 0.11; LightGBM R²: 0.69 RMSE: 0.11). Pairwise model comparison: Weighted Ensemble vs MLR not significantly different for total score; Weighted Ensemble vs CatBoost significant (t = −3.38, p < 0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GCT online task (Study 2; Chinese college students) the study leveraged fluency, flexibility, and originality process-derived indicators (including total operating time and composition range) to predict the creativity total score, finding that the Weighted Ensemble model achieved the best overall predictive fit (R² = 0.71, RMSE = 0.10) and outperformed CatBoost and LightGBM. This indicates that ensemble ML on process features can support more objective, scalable automated creativity scoring than manual rater aggregation, though the study is based on a recruited sample rather than a representative large-scale assessment design.

main_findings.dataset_used: GCT online task (Study 2; Chinese college students)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted Ensemble — R²: 0.79, RMSE: 0.10 (vs MLR R²: 0.78 RMSE: 0.10; CatBoost R²: 0.79 RMSE: 0.10; LightGBM R²: 0.78 RMSE: 0.10). Pairwise model comparison for fluency: Weighted Ensemble vs MLR significant (t = 3.07, p < 0.01), with Weighted Ensemble superior.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GCT online task (Study 2; Chinese college students) the study leveraged fluency-related process indicators (number of graphics, graphic movement times, number of colors used, and total operating time) to predict the fluency score, finding that the Weighted Ensemble model produced the highest fluency predictive accuracy (R² = 0.79, RMSE = 0.10) and significantly outperformed the linear baseline for fluency. This indicates that process-based behavioral features are especially informative for automating ideational fluency scoring, supporting faster feedback in online creativity assessment while still requiring careful validation against human judgments.

main_findings.dataset_used: GCT online task (Study 2; Chinese college students)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted Ensemble — R²: 0.65, RMSE: 0.12 (vs MLR R²: 0.66 RMSE: 0.12; CatBoost R²: 0.64 RMSE: 0.13; LightGBM R²: 0.62 RMSE: 0.13). The paper reports that MLR and Weighted Ensemble perform significantly better than CatBoost and LightGBM for dimension results, with no significant difference between MLR and Weighted Ensemble for flexibility.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GCT online task (Study 2; Chinese college students) the study leveraged flexibility process indicators (function key usage, changing scale, and rotation-related behaviors) to predict the flexibility score, finding that the Weighted Ensemble model achieved strong predictive fit (R² = 0.65, RMSE = 0.12) and performed at least as well as the linear baseline while exceeding the other nonlinear models. This indicates that automated flexibility scoring is feasible from interaction behaviors, which can reduce rater subjectivity and cost in large-scale online creativity screening.

main_findings.dataset_used: GCT online task (Study 2; Chinese college students)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted Ensemble — R²: 0.38, RMSE: 0.17 (vs MLR R²: 0.38 RMSE: 0.17; CatBoost R²: 0.38 RMSE: 0.17; LightGBM R²: 0.34 RMSE: 0.18). The paper notes originality has the weakest fit among dimensions (R² around 0.34–0.38), and the originality dimension is limited by having only two features.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GCT online task (Study 2; Chinese college students) the study leveraged originality process indicators (composition range and degree of overlap, plus related behavioral context) to predict the originality score, finding that predictive performance was weakest for originality (Weighted Ensemble R² = 0.38, RMSE = 0.17) compared with fluency and flexibility. This indicates that originality may require richer or more multidimensional behavioral features (beyond the current two-feature operationalization) to achieve reliable automated scoring, even when ensemble ML is used.

data.outcome_summary: This paper develops an online version of the Graphic Combination Task (GCT) and uses process-derived behavioral features to automate creativity scoring. In Study 1, an assessment framework was constructed and validated using expert ratings and criterion tasks; in Study 2, the 700 valid Chinese college participants’ process data were split 70%/30% for training/testing. Four ML models (MLR, CatBoost, LightGBM, and Weighted Ensemble) were compared using R² and RMSE on predicted expert-rated creativity outcomes. The Weighted Ensemble model performed best overall, achieving R² = 0.71 (RMSE = 0.10) for total creativity, R² = 0.79 (RMSE = 0.10) for fluency, R² = 0.65 (RMSE = 0.12) for flexibility, and R² = 0.38 (RMSE = 0.17) for originality. The study does not report a PV framework or a missing-data imputation strategy for ML inputs, and it uses a recruited sample rather than a probability-based large-scale assessment design, limiting generalizability.
